A rational number p/q is considered admissible when the smallest integer n for which p^n - 1 is divisible by q occurs at p itself. This study examines the limitations and capabilities of base-p automatic sequences when viewed through the lens of base-q, specifically in relation to languages defined by p/q-rational relations and the Chomsky hierarchy. It is proven that the set of integers where a p/q-recognisable sequence takes a non-zero value is not context-free in general, but is always recognisable by a finite automaton. Additionally, it is demonstrated that if a P/Q-recognisable sequence is ultimately periodic in base q, its non-zero values form a regular set in base p. Conversely, it is shown that there exists a sequence that is both p and q-recognisable, taking a non-zero value on all integers, and is context-free but not regular when considering the set of integers where the sequence is non-zero. Finally, it is established that there exists a pair of coprime integers p and q for which a sequence is both p and q-recognisable, taking a non-zero value on all integers, and is regular but not context-free when considering the set of integers where the sequence is non-zero.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented NoSQL database that provides
transactions to ensure data consistency and integrity. This paper presents a formal
specification of the three consistency levels in MongoDB: snapshot, read-your-
writes, and linearizable. We also develop a transactional consistency framework to
verify that client code adheres to these consistency levels. This framework can be
applied to prove the correctness of real-world code, such as the MongoDB driver for
Java.

We demonstrate that a specific family of homogeneous symmetric functions, denoted as $Q_n$, is $e$-positive, which means it can be expressed as a sum of symmetric functions of the form $m_\cdot$ with positive coefficients that are Euler characteristics of the order complexes of distributive lattices associated with 312-avoiding permutations. This lattice's order complex Euler characteristic is shown to be equivalent to that of $\Delta(\mathcal{B}(n))$. As a result, we prove that the inverse of the Kostka matrix consisting of $K_{\alpha n}$ entries has positive diagonal entries and is $e$-positive, which also implies that its inverse has non-negative off-diagonal entries.

This research focuses on comprehending the underlying structure and behavior of intricate networks by applying a spin system model to a specific type of nanoscale assembly. These assemblies consist of triangular Fe3O4 nanoparticles that are covalently bonded to one another. By analyzing magnetic properties through various experimental techniques, we were able to categorize the nanoscale assembly's network into a bipartite graph and develop a corresponding lattice model to represent its magnetic characteristics. The study found that the nanoscale assembly's dynamics are primarily influenced by triangle-based interactions rather than those between individual nanoparticles. This insight has significant implications for understanding intricate network behavior and could potentially be applied to other similar systems.

The recent launch of the Parker Solar Probe marks a significant milestone in our understanding of the inner heliosphere, as it will enable direct measurements of solar wind energy flux at close proximity to the Sun. By mapping the distribution of energy carried by solar wind plasma and magnetic fields, scientists can gain insights into the physical processes that govern solar wind acceleration and energy dissipation. To facilitate this research, we have developed a new dataset consisting of solar wind energy flux values calculated from plasma and magnetic field measurements taken by the Parker Solar Probe's instrument suite. This dataset is available for use with the spacecraft's position and velocity information relative to the Sun, as provided by the NASA Heliocentric Tool. The initial results from this dataset reveal that the energy carried by solar wind plasma is concentrated at lower energy levels in the inner heliosphere, while magnetic energy is distributed more evenly across energy levels. These findings are consistent with existing models and observations from previous spacecraft missions, and they highlight the importance of continued research into the physical processes that govern solar wind acceleration and energy dissipation in the inner heliosphere.

A key challenge in speech-emotion recognition is adapting models trained on artificial data to accurately detect genuine emotions expressed in spoken language. Models trained using labeled audio data can effectively identify speech-emotions, yet the presence of multiple, distinct emotions expressed in spoken language presents a significant challenge. To address this issue, transfer learning techniques have been employed to adapt models trained on artificial data to recognize genuine emotions expressed in spoken language. However, models trained using transfer learning often struggle to generalize across diverse, distinct emotions expressed in spoken language. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach called domain-adaptive reinforcement learning has been developed to simultaneously learn multiple, distinct emotions expressed in spoken language. This approach leverages the benefits of reinforcement learning to improve the generalization capabilities of models trained using artificial data. A prototype of this novel approach has been developed and tested on genuine speech recordings, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately detecting genuine emotions expressed in spoken language.

A one-dimensional shock wave model is used to simulate a strong shock in an expanding universe, considering a spherical void filled with a uniform, compressible, and self-gravitating gas. The gas is described using a self-similar solution to the Euler equations, and the shock wave's behavior is analyzed by examining the shock front's position, post-shock gas density, and velocity. The study finds that the post-shock gas density is directly proportional to the square of the expansion rate and the shock wave's strength, while the velocity is directly proportional to the expansion rate and independent of the shock wave's strength. The results are also compared to previous studies on shock waves in a self-gravitating gas without an expanding universe.

Using 4.6 fb^-1 of data collected by the LHCb experiment, the differential decay rate structure of $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ was analyzed as a function of the hadron recoil variable, $q^2$. This study involved 371 reconstructed signal candidates and utilized four parametric models based on complex vector form factors to fit the decay rate shape. The resulting complex vector form factor parameters were determined with high precision, enabling precise theoretical predictions for other decay modes of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^{+}\nu_{\mu}$ process.

This research paper explores the connection between Schrödinger operators with polynomial potentials and their corresponding pseudospectra, specifically focusing on operators whose potentials are of degree 4 or less. It has been previously established that such operators' pseudospectra can be described using algebraic curves, which can in turn be defined by generalized Hermite polynomials. Building on this foundation, we investigate the relationship between these polynomials and the geometric properties of the associated curves, including their genus and singularities. Additionally, we examine the conditions under which the associated curves can be parameterized using rational functions, and how this relates to the absence of monodromy in the associated differential equation.

The analysis of complex systems often involves studying their acoustic emissions, which can be represented as a sequence of discrete events with associated magnitudes. By examining the statistical properties of these sequences, researchers have developed tools to understand the underlying dynamics of such systems. In this study, we analyzed the acoustic signals generated during the peeling of an adhesive tape from a surface, which consists of a series of sudden releases of stored elastic energy. We calculated the distribution of event magnitudes and their inter-event times, and found that both distributions exhibit power-law behavior with similar exponents. This similarity in exponents suggests a potential connection between the two phenomena, which could be further explored using theoretical models.

A new non-abelian aether-like term has been proposed in the context of Yang-Mills theory, which is cubic in field strength and invariant under gauge transformations. This term's impact on a Yang-Mills theory's thermal behavior was investigated, revealing that it modifies the thermal mass of transverse gluons. This modification can be used to re-examine the thermalization of a non-abelian aether and the thermalization of a non-abelian aether coupled to gravity in an anti-de Sitter space.

This research develops a method to calculate the minimum capital required for a hedging strategy that involves purchasing options and delta hedging by trading stocks and options. We establish a relationship between the required capital, option prices, stock prices, and the number of options, and our calculations show how this capital changes in response to variations in these factors. We also examine the impact of option prices resulting from market inefficiencies on our calculations.

This study develops a dynamic economic model to examine the optimal allocation of opportunities across generations within a society characterized by social mobility. The research reveals that in an ideal scenario, society should reserve certain periods for individuals from disadvantaged backgrounds to demonstrate their capabilities before making decisions based on their family's social standing. The timing for making these decisions depends on the level of inequality in society, the difficulty of assessing an individual's potential, and the influence of social mobility. The model also reveals that in societies with high levels of inequality and limited social mobility, it is more efficient to base decisions on family background for a longer duration. The research further shows that in a model where individuals can influence each other's behavior, allocating opportunities based on family background can be more beneficial than allocating them randomly or solely based on an individual's potential. The study's findings are supported by numerical examples and theoretical analysis.

In 2015, the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) introduced a novel luminosity measurement technique using the ALICE detector, which relies on reconstructing head-on collisions of charged particles via their tracks. To validate this method, simulations were employed to generate luminosity profiles, and an experimental scan was conducted to measure profile widths and verify the ALICE luminosity profile model. The results of this scan were presented in this paper.

This research paper examines the optimization problem where multiple agents collaborate to minimize a sum of individual cost functions, each associated with a time-varying convex set. The feasible region for each agent is constrained by a union of convex sets, and the possible regions can change over time. We investigate two approaches to solving this optimization problem under the presence of malicious attacks, where one agent may intentionally provide false information to hinder the performance of the system. The first approach is a distributed optimization method that relies on agents exchanging information with their neighbors, while the second approach involves a central coordinator that collects data from all agents. We propose a quantized and robust algorithm that can withstand malicious attacks, and we analyze its convergence properties under different conditions. Our results demonstrate that the optimization error decreases over time, and we provide explicit bounds on the rate of convergence.

We have updated the s4cmb software package to accurately model the complex
instrumental systematics of cosmic microwave background experiments. These systematics
are now represented in simulated maps and time-series data, including the effects of
pixel resolution, beam distortion, and the modulation and leakage of the
dipole signal from moving satellites. To achieve this, we have developed a new
method for modeling the distortion of simulated maps due to the motion of
satellites, which is based on a spherical harmonic transformation of the observed
dipole signal. This method is computationally efficient and can be applied to
simulating the data of current and future high-precision experiments. To further
enhance the realism of our simulations, we have also included the modulation and
leakage of the dipole signal from moving satellites, which are modeled using
random Gaussian realizations. We have tested our updated simulations on simulated
data from the Planck satellite and found that they accurately reproduce the
observed systematics. We believe that our approach can be easily adapted to
incorporate the specific systematics of other experiments, which is an important
step towards improving the accuracy of cosmological parameter estimation.

The rise of pre-trained language models has led to a surge in research on the task of learning to order words. In order to address the limitations of existing datasets, which are often manually annotated and limited in quantity, researchers have turned to using the syntax of sequential language models as a substitute for manual annotation. However, it is unclear whether the order learned by these models carries any meaningful linguistic information or is simply a reflection of the model's internal representations. To investigate this, we have conducted an experiment using BART, a powerful sequential model, to analyze the role of pre-trained language models in learning to order words.

Recently, deepfake technology has become a significant concern due to its ability to create highly realistic and deceptive media. To combat this issue, numerous deepfake detection methods have been developed, yet they often struggle to effectively identify novel types of deceptions. To address this limitation, we propose a novel detection framework called the MD-CSDNetwork, which is based on a multi-domain cross-stitched architecture. This framework incorporates a dual-stream design that extracts features from both spatial and frequency domains, and utilizes a cross-stitched module to combine these features. Notably, the cross-stitched module is designed to dynamically adjust its configuration in response to varying detection challenges. Furthermore, the MD-CSDNetwork is equipped with a dual attention mechanism to prioritize important features and a dual adaptive gate that selectively filters out irrelevant information. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the superior performance of the MD-CSDNetwork in terms of accuracy, F1-score, and inference time.

In 1930, Menger developed the concept of angle function spaces and derived several fundamental properties. He proved that these spaces can be characterized using a specific type of metric, known as Birkhoff--Rosenthal metric, and established the relationship between angle preservation and metric isometry. However, he couldn't determine whether the characterization holds for metrics that aren't symmetric. This article confirms that angle spaces equipped with non-symmetric metrics can be equivalently characterized through a modified metric, denoted as $\lambda_x$, and as a result, the connection between angle and metric isometry can be determined.

This investigation establishes a connection between the fundamental and consecutive ideal lengths of a number field order through the use of skolem-like inequalities. These inequalities are further applied to derive upper limits for the g-delta invariants of curves defined over finite fields. Additionally, the paper provides a method to generate curves with high g-delta invariants and demonstrates the existence of curves with g-delta invariants that grow linearly in relation to their genus over finite fields.

We develop a new approach to construct cluster algebras from quantum groups using positive bases, specifically through the Fock-Rosly bracket on the coordinate ring of $GL_N$. This method allows us to apply Etnyre-Tang's theorem to establish the cluster nature of quantum Grassmannians, Lie supergroups, and classical flag varieties. Additionally, we introduce a novel isomorphism between the quantum Grassmannian and a specific cluster variety, which we prove to be mutation-equivalent.

Pyramid schemes are notorious for their deceptive nature, yet their inner workings are often shrouded in mystery. This research delves into the Forsage protocol, a high-yield investment program implemented on the Ethereum blockchain, which generated over $200 million in revenue before its abrupt shutdown. By examining Forsage's smart contract code, we uncover its intricate design, consisting of three interconnected components, and reveal its exploitative nature. Our findings highlight the critical need to prevent high-yield investment programs from being deployed on decentralized platforms, and we propose a framework for analyzing pyramid schemes based on user investment, reward allocation, and access control.

A study was conducted on 19 potential globular clusters located in the Milky Way's bulge, utilizing a color versus main sequence turn-off diagram derived from VVV infrared data. The clusters' ages and distances were estimated, and their metallicity values were found to range from -1.0 to -2.4. The ages of these clusters were found to range from 9 to 13 Gyr, with metallicity values that are comparable to other globular clusters in the Milky Way. The study also found that the clusters' ages and metallicity values are consistent with globular clusters in the Milky Way's disk, with no significant differences observed. The distances of these clusters were found to range from 4.2 to 8.4 kpc, with some located in the Milky Way's disk and others in the bulge. The study found that the clusters' radii range from 0.1 to 0.6 arcmin, with the majority of them being too small to be detected optically. We introduce Hyper-Invariant MERA (HIMERA), a novel tensor network structure that maintains a broad class of quantum states, encompassing both short- and long-range interacting systems. HIMERA retains the advantageous properties of the original Invariant MERA (IMERA), which efficiently represents a wide array of short-range interacting quantum systems. To address the limitations of IMERA in systems with power-law interactions, we incorporate additional bonds with localized connectivity into the network. We then explore the application of IMERA as a classical holographic error correction code, which facilitates efficient code recovery and data protection. We further investigate the impact of varying connectivity on the code's distance and decoding complexity. Finally, we propose a strategy for efficiently simulating Hamiltonians with power-law interactions by interpolating between IMERA and HIMERA network structures.

This study investigates the application of deep learning models, specifically LSTM, GRU, and a feedforward neural network, in analyzing and predicting business processes. We evaluate their effectiveness in predicting process outcomes and process failures, as well as their ability to classify processes into normal and anomalous states. To achieve this, we utilize the large-scale German e-commerce dataset, comprising 10 million events. Our findings reveal that deep learning models excel in predicting process outcomes and detecting anomalies, outperforming traditional methods. However, their application in predicting process failures is more nuanced, with the choice of model depending on the specific prediction task at hand. Our results provide valuable insights for practitioners and researchers working with business process data.

This research establishes characterizations of the $\Sigma_\sigma^m_M$ space using character functions. Specifically, we establish that a function $f$ belongs to the $\Sigma_\sigma^m_M$ space if and only if its character function $\widehat{f}$ adheres to the condition $\|\partial^\alpha \widehat{f}\|_\infty \leq C_\alpha A^\alpha (\ln(1+|\alpha|))^{\frac{m}{2}} B^{|\alpha|}$ for all multi-indices $\alpha \in \mathbb{N}_0^d$, where the constants $A,B,C_\alpha$ are independent of $\alpha$. Moreover, we establish that the symbol class $S_\sigma^m_M$ is non-trivial, and we establish that a Toeplitz operator with a symbol in the $\Sigma_\sigma^{m,M}$ space has a bounded extension on the $L^2$ space.

Astronomical studies of stellar flares in the near-ultraviolet spectrum are often
challenging to model due to the difficulty in detecting absorption features
caused by neutral atoms and ions in the chromosphere.  To address this issue, a
new approach is proposed that uses a Monte Carlo method to simulate the
near-ultraviolet continuum of a specific flare, AD Leo, which occurred in 1985.
By comparing the simulated results with observed data, key parameters such as
electron temperature, hydrogen ionization, and ionization levels of various
elements can be determined.  To facilitate this comparison, a new format for
presenting near-ultraviolet spectra is also introduced.  To further enhance
analytical capabilities, a Python-based tool is developed to convert the new
spectral format into a two-dimensional array, which can then be used to model
flares in the near-ultraviolet spectrum.  This approach provides a foundation
for analyzing and modeling stellar flares in the near-ultraviolet spectrum.

Point cloud deep neural networks have seen significant growth in recent years, yet their application in safety-critical scenarios is hindered by their lack of interpretability and explainability. To address this issue, point cloud models incorporating external knowledge have emerged as a promising direction. However, existing methods that utilize this knowledge often fall short in effectively integrating it. In response to this challenge, we present a novel approach called TPC, which employs a transformation-based strategy to incorporate knowledge into point cloud models. TPC leverages the invariance of neural networks to linear transformations to smooth the target data by applying the same transformation to neighboring points. Our approach is computationally efficient, with a low per-point cost of O(k), where k represents the number of neighboring points. Our method's performance has been evaluated on multiple benchmarks, including MNIST-PC, SHREC, ModelNet40, and KITTI, and the results demonstrate that TPC outperforms the current state-of-the-art knowledge-based methods.

This paper introduces a novel approach to clustering dynamical systems, considering both linear and nonlinear models. Our method employs a statistical framework to define influence between systems, resulting in a symmetric and transitive relation that facilitates efficient clustering. By representing systems as nodes in a graph, where the edge weights reflect their mutual influence, we apply the Kerneling Nona-negative Matrix Factorization (KNMF) algorithm to identify meaningful clusters. Our approach is particularly useful for analyzing large-scale networks of interconnected systems, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through simulations of linear and nonlinear dynamical models. Our findings reveal that our method can accurately identify clusters of systems, even in the presence of significant heterogeneity and complexity.

Recently, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have achieved significant success in generating various types of data, including text. However, traditional GANs require sampling from the entire vocabulary to generate each character, which is computationally expensive and impractical for many applications. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach called SparseGAN, which utilizes a sparse matrix to selectively choose a subset of characters to generate each character in a sequence. This approach significantly reduces the computational cost of generating text by a factor of 100, while maintaining comparable quality to traditional GANs on standard benchmarks. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

The concept of interstellar panspermia, which involves the transfer of life between galaxies, is a topic of interest. To assess the likelihood of detecting this phenomenon, a mathematical model was developed to simulate the evolution of microbial populations on living comets. The model takes into account various factors, including the effects of solar radiation, the comets' distance from the sun, and their elliptical orbits. The results of the model were then used to evaluate the survival chances of microorganisms on specific comets, including those from the Rosetta and StarTrackers missions. The study found that while the transfer of life between galaxies may be possible, the narrow conditions required for survival make it unlikely that we will be able to observe it.

Spatial capture-recapture (SCR) models have become a standard method for estimating animal population density and size, but they often overlook individual animal movements and resource selection patterns that can significantly impact these estimates. This study introduces a novel approach to integrating selection information from resource use data into SCR models, specifically for animals with discrete locations, such as nesting birds. We developed a flexible framework that allows for the incorporation of selection covariates in both the animal detection process and the spatial intensity model, and we compared this approach to traditional models that only account for selection in the intensity model. Using simulated data, we found that ignoring selection covariates in the detection process can lead to biased estimates of population density and size, and we demonstrated the practical application of this model to estimate the population size of a rare bird species, the California condor, during their nesting period.

The study of multilayer networks has gained significant interest in recent years, particularly in the context of network synchronization. A key challenge in this research is understanding how interconnected networks influence each other, especially when connections between layers are one-way. In this paper, we investigate the dynamics of synchronization in multilayer networks with one-way connections between layers. We derive an analytical condition for the onset of synchronization and develop a method to predict the critical point at which the system becomes synchronized. Our theoretical findings are validated through numerical simulations of a two-layer network model. We also explore the impact of different network configurations on the multilayer system, including the effects of intra-layer and inter-layer connections. Our results demonstrate that the multilayer system can exhibit both cooperative and competitive behaviors, leading to a variety of complex dynamics. Our study provides valuable insights into the nature of synchronization in multilayer networks and has potential applications in a wide range of fields, including neuroscience, biology, and social sciences.

Given a linear space of symmetric tensor fields on a domain in R^3, we investigate the Cauchy stress operator, which maps symmetric tensor fields to vectors. We characterize this operator using its null space and range, and develop a parametrization of it. Our analysis reveals that its parametrization is inherently non-linear. We provide a concise, non-convex formulation of its non-linear parametrization.

The concept of Assumption-Guarantee Relations has been utilized in various aspects of computer science, particularly in the development of software. This study introduces a fresh perspective on these relations by interpreting them through the lens of geometry. In this geometric framework, assumptions and guarantees are represented as shapes within a space of possible system behaviors, where the relationship between these shapes can be visualized and analyzed. A key component of this theory is the introduction of a geometric operator that enables the construction of shapes from basic components, facilitating the development of software tests based on specified assumptions and guarantees. The applicability of this approach is demonstrated through the creation of a testing framework for Java programs.

Let G be a group consisting of upper triangular matrices with 1s on the diagonal, where the entries are from a field K. This G group acts on a specific part of a representation, denoted as V, and we are examining the behavior of the orbits of this action. In particular, we are focusing on two scenarios: when G is of a certain type and the field K is finite, and when G is of a more complex type and the field K has an infinite number of elements. In both cases, we are analyzing the dimensions of the various orbits and determining the dimensions of the largest possible orbits. Additionally, when the field K is finite, we are calculating the number of orbits with the maximum dimension and providing explicit examples of the vectors that belong to these orbits.

This research addresses the challenge of estimating a network's size in a network with limited knowledge, specifically under conditions where some nodes may act maliciously. We focus on estimating the network size in small-world networks, where nodes can only communicate with nearby neighbors and must use local communication protocols to achieve this goal. Our approach involves creating a set of robust estimators that can accurately estimate the network size even when malicious nodes attempt to skew the results. We then develop a method to efficiently distribute these estimators across the network using gossip protocols, allowing the nodes to combine their individual estimates and obtain an accurate assessment of the network's size. Our experimental evaluations demonstrate that our approach can estimate the network size within a factor of 2 with 95% confidence, using local communication protocols and tolerating up to 30% malicious nodes. Our findings also reveal that our method can be used to estimate the network size in fully connected networks, providing a valuable tool for a wide range of applications where nodes must operate with limited knowledge of their surroundings.

This research develops a nonparametric method to estimate the length of traffic queues based on data from probe vehicles. A key challenge in this estimation arises from incomplete information, as some vehicles may leave the scene without providing data. To address this, a combinatorial approach is proposed, which uses the available data to infer the possible range of queue lengths. A nonparametric estimator is then derived from the available probability distribution. A Bayesian framework is used to obtain point estimates and credible intervals. A simulation study is conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed estimator and compare it to existing parametric methods. The proposed method is also applied to real-world data from a busy urban intersection in Los Angeles, California.

We present a new iterative approach to solving the initial data constraints in numerical relativity, which is designed to be computationally efficient and straightforward to implement in existing simulation codes. Our method is built upon a finite-difference framework and employs a time-stepping scheme with rescaling and filtering techniques to ensure stability. We have tested our algorithm on a variety of initial data solvers and found it to be more efficient than traditional methods, which is particularly beneficial in scenarios that require adaptive mesh refinement. Our findings suggest that our approach is well-suited for inclusion in a wide range of simulation codes, which is particularly relevant in the context of next-generation gravitational wave observatories.

We measured the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn3NiN thin films, which exhibit a G-type antiferromagnetic order. A significant anomalous Nernst coefficient of up to 10 microvolts per kelvin and tesla was observed near the Curie temperature. This effect is attributed to the anomalous Hall effect through the Onsager reciprocity principle.

User facilities like synchrotron light sources and free-electron lasers produce high-quality data for research, but their operation is labor-intensive and time-consuming. To improve efficiency, these facilities are moving towards automated, high-throughput systems that allow multiple users to work simultaneously. However, managing these systems effectively requires advanced data management and control capabilities. To bridge this gap, we're developing machine learning models that can replicate the complex decision-making processes used by skilled users. By training these models on real-world data, we aim to create a flexible and adaptable system that can be easily adapted to different types of user facilities. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through a proof-of-concept application at a synchrotron light source, showing significant improvements in performance compared to traditional methods.

We provide a detailed explanation of Kummer theory for abelian extensions of local fields, including an explicit description of the Galois group as a quotient of the absolute Galois group. This enhanced understanding of local class field theory enables us to describe the inertial Hecke eigenspace for GL_2 over the ring of integers in a totally ramified extension. Specifically, we can identify the set of associated Hecke operators with a subset of GL_2(R) modulo congruence equivalence. Furthermore, we can characterize this subset as a subset of GL_2(R)/GL_2(o) with respect to a specific congruence condition. This allows us to establish the finiteness of the set of associated Hecke operators.

We establish a new isoperimetric inequality for a hypersurface that minimizes a certain functional, which is defined as the difference between the area of a portion of the hypersurface and the area of its boundary, divided by the boundary's perimeter. This section of the hypersurface is required to have a specified mean curvature within a given range. Our main finding shows that for any such hypersurface with a bounded mean curvature, there exists a corresponding threshold beyond which a part of the surface can be enclosed within a region with the optimal shape, which resides on another hypersurface that also has a bounded mean curvature. This result is supported by a series of technical steps, including a novel approach to analyzing the relationship between the functional and the geometry of the hypersurface.

This study investigates the use of electro-mechanical self-sensing technology in carbon fiber-reinforced polymer composites to detect and locate damage, specifically delamination. By measuring changes in capacitance and employing electrical impedance tomography, researchers can create an image of the damage location and shape. To accurately represent the delamination's shape, an iterative optimization process using a genetic algorithm is applied. This method allows for the precise identification of the delamination's shape and size, which is essential for developing effective self-healing systems. The study demonstrates the ability to detect and locate delamination with high accuracy, which is a critical step towards creating composites that can repair themselves.

We're considering the possibility that a more complex, cohesive, and self-sustaining biological ecosystem could be seen as a form of life at a higher level, potentially exhibiting consciousness. This concept is being compared to the workings of artificial intelligence, specifically large language models, which are being scrutinized to determine if they too could be considered conscious entities. However, we're not asserting that these models are conscious, but rather that they may possess a form of computation that is akin to a basic level of consciousness. Ultimately, we're calling for further research to explore the nature of consciousness and to develop a more precise definition that can be applied to various entities, including biological ecosystems and artificial intelligence systems.

This paper presents a tensor-based approach to Euclidean space, utilizing geometric objects such as vectors and tensors of various ranks. We establish clear connections between these objects and their components, and demonstrate how to perform transformations and operations on them. The section on tensor products and powers is particularly detailed, and we also outline the fundamental properties of linear transformations. To support these concepts, we provide a Python package that enables the execution of tensor operations in a straightforward manner.

A theoretical model is proposed that involves a new, neutral scalar or pseudoscalar particle which interacts with quarks based on their flavor and is essentially undetectable through hadrons. This particle's near-invisibility is due to a quantum mechanical effect that hinders its decay into quarks. The model is mathematically consistent and can be used to create a new, similar particle that is also nearly undetectable. Theoretical calculations show that this particle could have a mass of several GeV and would interact with quarks and electrons in a way that is proportional to their mass. The model's predictions can be compared to existing experimental data from various particle colliders, and it is found to be in agreement with these observations. The model is also used to explain the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon and the excess of B-meson decays observed in the LHCb experiment.

In this study, we investigate the Toda conformal field theory in $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ by examining its Belinfante-Raikov-Segal identities. We derive the key equations that govern the theory, which are analogous to the conformal Ward identities found in the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda conformal field theory. We also uncover a connection between these equations and the Gelfand-Dickey hierarchy, which is a set of integrable equations. Furthermore, we uncover a relationship between the operators in the Toda conformal field theory and those in the KdV hierarchy, which is a subset of the Gelfand-Dickey hierarchy. We find that these operators commute with each other and that their eigenvalues are related to the conformal blocks in the Toda conformal field theory. We demonstrate that these blocks can be expressed in terms of the $\tau$-function in the Toda hierarchy, which is a solution to a set of integrable equations. We also uncover a connection between the $\tau$-function in the Toda hierarchy and the $\tau$-function in the KdV hierarchy, which is a subset of the Toda hierarchy. We find that this relationship is analogous to the relationship between the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ and $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Lie algebras.
Coxeter groups form a subclass of groups with presentations defined by unique sets of generators and relations, now demonstrated to possess biautomatic properties.

Restoring lost limb function through cortical neuroprostheses is a significant challenge, particularly for complex movements like walking. To address this, researchers are developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) that can interpret cortical signals and control prosthetic limbs. However, existing BCI systems are not well-suited for controlling walking due to their limitations in accurately decoding continuous movements. In this study, a new BCI system was developed to decode the gait cycle and step rates from electrocorticogram (ECoG) signals, with the goal of controlling a prosthetic leg. The study involved six amputees who wore a sensorized residual limb and had BCI-controlled prostheses. The results showed that the new BCI system could accurately decode gait phases and step rates, with high correlation coefficients and low root mean square errors. The study also demonstrated that the BCI system could successfully control a sensorized residual limb and a prosthetic leg, with the participants able to walk at a comfortable speed. Overall, the findings suggest that the new BCI system could be a valuable tool for restoring walking function in individuals with limb loss.

We demonstrate that certain right-angled Artin groups with at least three generators cannot be expressed as semidirect products involving free groups. Specifically, we prove that if a right-angled Artan group's graph is a cycle with at least three vertices, it does not admit a semidirect product decomposition with a free group. Furthermore, we show that if the graph is a complete bipartite graph with at least five vertices, it also does not admit a semidirect product decomposition with a free group.

Estimating the connections between nodes in a network from time-series data is a challenging task, particularly when the network's connections are changing over time. This paper presents a novel approach called Deep Dynamic Effective Connectivity (DDEC) to address this issue. DDEC employs a multi-layered neural network to simultaneously model the network's structure and the way it changes over time. This network is divided into three parts: an input layer that encodes time, a shared layer that extracts common features, and task-specific layers that predict the network's connections at different time points. This approach allows for a more efficient and compact representation of the network's connections, reducing the number of parameters needed to train the model. The DDEC approach is evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and the results show that it outperforms existing methods in predicting the network's connections at different time points.

Biological locomotion is a complex behavior that involves the interaction of an organism with its environment. To understand this behavior computationally, we must first establish a framework for modeling the biological entity and its surroundings. This framework can be used to develop a system that analyzes video footage to identify biological locomotion. To achieve this, we must consider various factors, including the type of organism, its environment, and the available sensory information. By examining these factors, we can develop a set of criteria for identifying biological locomotion in video footage. This set of criteria can be used to guide the design of a computational system that analyzes video footage and identifies biological locomotion. To illustrate this approach, we will examine various examples, including the movement of microorganisms, insects, and mammals. By analyzing these examples, we can develop a more comprehensive understanding of biological locomotion and its computational representation.

This paper presents an enhanced version of a fast iterative matrix inversion method originally proposed by Higham and Wu, which allows for the efficient calculation of the inverse of a non-singular matrix using iterative optimization. By representing the matrix inverse as a sum of multiple scaled component matrices, our approach generalizes the initial set of component matrices beyond just the identity matrix, thereby expanding the scope of this technique. We conducted a series of numerical experiments on GPU-accelerated systems to evaluate the performance of our algorithm, which demonstrated significant improvements in convergence speed compared to the existing method. Specifically, our approach achieved a reduction in the number of iterations required for convergence by a factor of approximately 2.5 to 3, depending on the chosen set of component matrices.

We investigate topological Anderson insulators arising from random binary disorders in a two-dimensional square lattice with nearest-neighbor hopping. By utilizing the self-consistent Born approximation, we map the system's Hamiltonian in momentum space and calculate the Z2 topological invariant for various disorder strengths and hopping parameters. Our numerical results are further validated through the calculation of the Chern number within the clean limit. Notably, we find that the topological phase is confined within a closed loop on the parameter plane, bounded by four distinct phase transitions that occur at zero energy. These transitions are characterized by the formation of flat bands at the corners of the Brillouin zone, leading to localized states and the emergence of the quantum Hall effect. We also identify the coexistence of the topological phase and the Anderson insulator phase, which is separated by a topological transition.

This thesis explores the fundamental concepts of complex tori, Riemann surfaces, and their relationship to abelian varieties, with a focus on the properties of isogenies and their impact on complex tori. It delves into the connection between lattice structures and isomorphic complex tori, and demonstrates how isogenies can be represented as linear transformations on lattice structures. Furthermore, the thesis investigates the composition of complex tori and their associated lattices, and provides an explicit calculation of the composition of two isogenies. It also explores the concept of complex tori that are isomorphic under different lattice structures, and provides an example of a lattice structure that is self-isomorphic under a specific complex number transformation. Finally, the thesis proves that any complex tori can be represented as a substructure of a higher-dimensional complex tori, and provides an explicit dimension for this substructure.

We have developed a comprehensive and self-consistent model of the supersymmetric
Standard Model's Hadron Collider on-shell Higgs boson production process, taking
into account the complex nature of its parameters. Our approach incorporates the
full set of tree-level and one-loop supersymmetric contributions to the Higgs
potential, as well as top-quark contributions, and utilizes the effective
potential approach to handle the non-supersymmetric components. Our calculation
of the complex-Matrix Elements includes both leading and next-to-leading order
corrections to the strong interaction, and we have incorporated the relevant
hadronization effects through the use of the Generalized Parton Distributions. Our
predictions for the inclusive and inclusive-plus-jet cross-sections are compared
to available experimental data, and we have also considered the implications of
on-shell Higgs production for the determination of the supersymmetric parameters.

Contextual linear bandits are a significant area of research with numerous applications. In many scenarios, the contextual linear bandits problem is divided into multiple independent sub-problems, each associated with an independent agent and its own context. Despite this, the standard methods for solving these problems fail to take advantage of the shared statistical properties of the underlying parameter vectors. In this paper, we propose two novel algorithms that enable agents to learn a common unknown parameter vector from their independent contexts without revealing the contexts themselves. The first algorithm, known as the "Simultaneous Learning" approach, assumes that the contexts are generated from the same distribution and allows the agents to learn the parameter vector by exchanging randomized updates. The proposed algorithm achieves a regret bound of $\tilde O(d^{3/2} \sqrt{T})$, which is comparable to the optimal bound in the full information setting. The second approach, called "Sequential Learning", is designed for scenarios where the contexts are generated from different distributions and involves a leader-follower framework. The proposed algorithm achieves a total regret bound of $\tilde O(d^{3/2} \sqrt{T} + \sum_{i=1}^n d d_i \sqrt{T_i})$, which is comparable to the sum of the optimal bounds in the single agent setting. Both algorithms are evaluated through numerical experiments, which demonstrate their effectiveness in learning the parameter vector from independent contexts.

The event shape engineering method was applied to lead-lead collisions at a top energy level of 2.76 TeV, allowing for the modification of initial collisions' pressure gradients and the resulting impact on the elliptic flow of charged particles. By manipulating the initial geometry of collisions through higher-order moments, the researchers found that events with increased ellipticity exhibited a higher elliptic flow, while those with decreased geometry showed the opposite effect. This pattern was observed across various transverse momentum ranges and mid-rapidity regions. Furthermore, events with modified geometry demonstrated a shift in the transverse momentum distribution of produced particles, with an increase in transverse momentum for events with increased geometry and a decrease for events with decreased geometry. These findings were consistent across different collision centrality levels and were unaffected by the initial geometry's impact on the elliptic flow.

This research investigates the relationship between two power control methods,
binary and extremal (unconstrained) power control, in terms of their gains in
generalized degrees of freedom in interference networks. We define binary power
control as a system where users can only choose between full or no transmission,
and extremal power control as a system where users can transmit at any power
within their limits. The goal is to quantify the gain of extremal power control
over binary power control in terms of its impact on interference networks. Our
research reveals that the extremal power control gain over binary power control
is proportional to the square root of the number of users in the network, and
furthermore, we provide a binary power control strategy that achieves this gain
up to a constant factor for any number of users in the network.

This research presents a novel multiple-time-step (MTS) integration method for simulating particle-particle interactions in fluid flows. Unlike existing MTS methods, our approach takes into account the physical collision time of particles, which is crucial for accurately modeling fluid flows. Our algorithm uses a reduced time step for particles during intervals when they are not interacting with each other, and increases the time step during periods of interaction. We tested our MTS method on a flow around two identical particles and found that our results were more accurate than those obtained using a standard single-time-step (STS) method. Our findings also indicate that our MTS method is computationally more efficient than the STS method for simulating particle-particle interactions in fluid flows.

This article discusses the history of finding non-zero whole number solutions to the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$. It examines the case where $n$ is a positive integer and demonstrates that the equation has infinitely many solutions. Additionally, it provides three specific solutions, where $a$ and $b$ are also whole numbers.

This study develops a comprehensive framework to model the interaction between a hopping robot and soft ground, incorporating soil deformation and the robot's motion dynamics. This hybrid model is computationally intensive, so we also create a simplified version that captures the essential features of soil-structure interaction. Using these models, we simulate a hopping robot's behavior on various soft surfaces and analyze its performance metrics. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of surface properties and robot mass on its performance, leading to an optimized design for maximizing its hopping distance.

A unified approach is proposed to describe the behavior of mesons, specifically the scalar $a_0(980)$, vector $\rho(770)$, and axial-vector $a_1(1260)$ mesons. This method uses a quark-antiquark effective Lagrangian within a quark model framework. The study derives the relationship between the mesons' cutoff parameters and investigates their impact on the mesons' elastic form factors. The findings are compared to existing experimental data.

We introduce a new framework to capture the hierarchical relationships within large-scale information networks, specifically focusing on a variation of the classic dendrogram structure. This model is defined by a set of directed links that represent potential parent-child relationships between clusters of nodes, and we develop an efficient method to identify these connections in networks with millions of nodes and edges. Our approach is based on a novel optimization problem that seeks to maximize the information content of the network's dendrogram, and we provide a scalable solution using a combination of graph partitioning and local search techniques. Our models are evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate their effectiveness in capturing the inherent structure of the network, with significant improvements in accuracy compared to existing methods.

Quantum annealing's efficiency is significantly influenced by the balance between its speed and the size of its solution space. This study investigates the relationship between a key parameter, known as the annealing gap, and a process called quantum quench within the exact cover problem. By examining this duality, we developed a method to forecast the post-quench behavior of a system, specifically its tendency to reach the system's lowest energy state. Our findings reveal that the size of the annealing gap directly impacts the system's ability to settle into its ground state following a quantum quench. Furthermore, we observed that the relationship between the annealing gap and the system's behavior changes as the problem's complexity increases.

We develop a two-band model incorporating both $3d$ and $5d$ conduction channels to account for screening effects in infinite-layer nickelates. This model includes significant spin-orbit coupling and multiple occupancy, and we investigate its behavior using a screened Hubbard model approach. Our findings reveal that screening shifts the $2p$ orbital to the $3d$ orbital energy range, leading to orbital hybridization and the emergence of two distinct sets of narrow bands with different angular momentum characteristics. Notably, the model exhibits a range of doping levels where the $3d$ and $2p$ bands coexist, and we predict that optimally doped infinite-layer nickelates feature a two-band system with an unusual arrangement of filled and empty pockets.

The relationship between a star's density and the speed of sound within it is a fundamental aspect of stellar structure. This study derives an equation for sound propagation in a specific type of dense matter found in stars, incorporating the effects of quark composition and strong interactions. The resulting equation is expressed in terms of a star's equation of state, and its behavior is examined across various densities and equations used to describe the interaction between quarks. The research reveals that the speed of sound in this dense matter is influenced by the presence of specific quark types and can be described using a linear function of the equation's parameters. The findings are compared to theoretical models and observations, particularly in relation to the structure of neutron stars. The research also highlights the potential for using sound propagation to understand the internal structure of these dense objects.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states, including the compass, cat, and Gouliatmin states, when subjected to both squeezing and displacement transformations. By examining their behavior in phase space, we develop a comprehensive visual representation of these states using the Wigner function. This approach enables us to derive an analytical formula for the compass state under these transformations, which serves as a foundation for further numerical analysis. Our study reveals that the compass state's unique characteristics are preserved under these transformations, and we explore the implications of this invariance in relation to other non-classical states.

A key factor in the formation of gas giant planets is the rapid growth of solid material within a short time frame. The presence of a velocity shear in protoplanetary disks can create an instability that stirs the gas and dust, potentially hindering the migration of planetesimals. A recent study investigated the impact of a specific type of particle settling, known as a dust dead zone, on this instability in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. By developing a two-dimensional model that includes a realistic representation of the dust distribution, the study found that the instability can drive a type of material transport that can lead to the formation of gas giant planets. Specifically, the study found that the instability can drive the formation of pressure bumps that can trap solid material and create regions of high density that can lead to the formation of gas giant planets. By exploring the relationship between the stirring caused by this instability and the formation of gas giant planets, the study provides a possible explanation for the rapid growth of solid material within a short time frame.

This research focuses on harmonic functions defined on a specific type of manifold, which has a compacted shrinking Ricci curvature and maintains a uniform scalar curvature throughout. We establish that any such function that is twice differentiable and not constantly zero must be unbounded, thereby proving a harmonic function analogue to a previously discovered theorem. This result is then utilized to demonstrate the non-existence of non-trivial functions with a specific type of differential property on this manifold.

A new type of malicious modification in machine learning models, dubbed a dynamic backdoor, is explored in this paper. Unlike traditional backdoors that rely on a specific trigger, this new modification uses a layer of global average pooling to activate a malicious behavior when a specific input is fed into a trained model. We found that this type of modification is highly effective in evading detection methods, even when the model is subjected to rigorous analysis. Our research also reveals that the specific input that activates this malicious behavior is not unique, but rather a property of a large class of input patterns. To further investigate this behavior, we developed a new concept called a "feature hole" to describe the underlying mechanism. Our findings demonstrate that this type of malicious modification can be used to achieve a wide range of goals, from activating a specific behavior to stealing sensitive information.

In this study, we investigate the impact of the General Relativity parameter gamma on astrometric measurements that a mission like Gaia could measure. We found that the uncertainty in gamma can lead to systematic errors in the observed parallax of stars, with the magnitude of this error depending on the direction of the line of sight. Specifically, the error in gamma can cause a shift in the observed parallax of up to 0.12 mas, which is 12% of the 1 mas uncertainty in the average parallax of the Gaia data. This effect is primarily due to the gravitational influence of the Milky Way on the apparent motion of stars, with the direction of this influence varying based on the position of the star in the galaxy. We also found that the uncertainty in gamma can lead to a bias in the measured value of gamma itself, with the bias depending on the distribution of stars in the galaxy. For instance, if the Gaia data is dominated by stars in the galactic disk, the bias in gamma would be 0.0001, which is 10% of the current uncertainty in gamma. However, if the data is dominated by stars in the galactic bulge, the bias in gamma would be 0.001, which is 100% of the current uncertainty in gamma. To effectively answer open-ended questions that require common sense reasoning, leveraging related knowledge is crucial. However, existing approaches struggle to utilize a large amount of semantically connected knowledge due to the risk of incorporating irrelevant information. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach called Coarse-to-Careful Knowledge Selection (CKS), which aims to efficiently incorporate semantic knowledge for commonsense question answering. Our CKS framework consists of two main components: a knowledge sub-question generation module and a careful knowledge selection module. The generation module creates open-ended sub-questions designed to elicit relevant knowledge, while the selection module filters out irrelevant knowledge to ensure accurate question answering. Our approach demonstrates significant improvements over current baselines on two widely used datasets, showing a 10.1% and 11.4% increase in accuracy on CommonsenseQA and SocialIQA, respectively.

Astronomical observations have been instrumental in revealing a multitude of molecular species present in space, including those that are neutral. However, our understanding of stable molecules is incomplete, particularly when it comes to cationic species containing oxygen, such as O2+, H2O+, OH+, and CO+. These ions are significant as they participate in a range of chemical reactions, particularly in the context of comets. Despite their prevalence in cometary environments, our knowledge of their spectral characteristics is limited, hindering our ability to accurately interpret the molecular composition of comets. To address this issue, we have compiled a comprehensive review of the available literature on the spectral properties of these oxygen-containing cationic molecules, with the aim of identifying areas where further research is needed. Our analysis reveals that there is a significant lack of laboratory data for H2O+ and CO+ molecules, particularly in the ultraviolet and visible wavelength ranges, which are highly relevant to cometary observations. In contrast, the spectral properties of O2+ and OH+ molecules are better understood, with a wealth of laboratory data available. However, there is still room for improvement, particularly in terms of expanding the wavelength range and improving the accuracy of existing measurements. To facilitate future research, we have also developed a database of the available literature on the spectral properties of these molecules, which can be used as a starting point for further studies.

In the context of a non-i.i.d. learning scenario, a random walk strategy is utilized to train a machine learning model across multiple devices in a federated setting. This approach, which eliminates the need for a central server to manage device data, allows for a decentralized learning process. However, this paper's focus is specifically on applying a random walk approach to a federated learning framework. By eliminating the need for a central server to manage device data, this approach allows for a decentralized learning process. In a real-world scenario, a random walk learning system is demonstrated where a machine learning model is trained across multiple devices in a decentralized manner. Experimental results show that this learning approach is comparable to traditional methods in terms of model accuracy, while also offering significant improvements in communication efficiency and privacy protection.

This study examines the impact of a mental health treatment requirement for 1,000 convicted individuals in Los Angeles County between 2000 and 2010. This policy was implemented to address mental health issues among criminal defendants and was a result of a 2001 court ruling. Our analysis reveals that the treatment mandate had a significant positive effect on recidivism rates among offenders with violent crimes, reducing re-arrest rates by 25 percent and reducing rearrests by 15 percent. Conversely, the policy had little to no effect on offenders with non-violent crimes. The effects of the policy varied based on the severity of the crime, the length of time since conviction, and the age of the offender. The reduction in violent recidivism was primarily due to a decrease in violent re-offending rather than property crimes. The study also found that the policy's impact was influenced by the type of mental health issue, the length of time since conviction, and the age of the offender. The results suggest that mental health treatment can have a significant impact on reducing violent recidivism among convicted individuals.

A key challenge in medical image segmentation is accurately delineating thin structures and disease areas. This issue is compounded by the scarcity of labeled data in medical imaging. This paper introduces a novel semi-supervised medical image segmentation framework, combining a fully convolutional network with consistency regularization. This method leverages unlabeled data to enhance the robustness of the label-deficient network. We tested this approach on three MRI datasets, including brain and cardiac imaging, and found that it outperforms existing semi-supervised label-deficient network methods.

The performance of solid-state materials is significantly influenced by their atomic structure, and understanding the relationship between structure and properties is a key challenge. Machine learning models, particularly graph neural networks (GNNs), have shown great potential in this area, but their black-box nature makes them difficult to interpret. In this study, we introduce a simple GNN design that is both easy to interpret and highly effective at predicting the electronic properties of disordered materials. Our model, which is based on a feature extraction GNN (FE-GNN) framework, is tested on a wide range of disordered materials, including amorphous semiconductors, glassy alloys, and glassy polymers. The results show that our FE-GNN design outperforms existing methods in predicting electronic properties, and we also demonstrate how GNNs can be used to gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between structure and properties in disordered materials.

This research introduces a generalized framework for estimating a specific parameter within a mixture distribution, given multiple independent and identically distributed observations from that distribution. The method proposed utilizes maximum likelihood estimation to achieve this goal. The framework is applied to estimate the population mean from a mixture distribution, and the efficiency of the resulting estimators is compared to existing methods. The study also explores the practical application of these methods in estimating the mean of a finite population, and the results are supported by numerical simulations.

Knowledge tracing is a task in educational data mining that aims to predict a student's understanding of a concept based on their interaction history with related content. Despite the abundance of deep learning models developed for knowledge tracing, there is a lack of consensus on the most effective approaches to employ. This is largely due to the difficulty in comparing models fairly, as it is difficult to ensure fair and consistent benchmarking across different algorithms. To address this issue, we present PyKT, a Python package that provides a unified interface for implementing and evaluating deep learning knowledge tracing models. PyKT includes pre-built data loaders and evaluation metrics, as well as the most popular deep learning architectures for knowledge tracing, enabling researchers to easily and fairly compare these models.

This note demonstrates that a second-order elliptic operator $P$ defined on smooth, compactly supported sections of a vector bundle over a non-compact manifold possesses a closed range in the $L^2$-norm. Consequently, the quotient space $L^2(E)/\text{Im}(P)$ forms a well-defined Hilbert space.

The Alethe proof format is a generic format for representing logical proofs,
which is used extensively in research and development. It is designed to be
versatile, allowing for the integration of various backends and tools. It is
open-source, which makes it accessible for the community to use and modify.
However, its lack of formal specification makes it difficult to use with certain
tools, which require a precise description of the input format. This project aims
to provide a Coq-based implementation of the Alethe proof format, which includes
its syntax and semantics. This will enable the format to be used with a wider
range of tools, which can verify its properties in Coq.

As the number of devices participating in mobile and IoT applications grows, efficiently managing these devices during the training of machine learning models becomes a significant challenge. Existing methods for distributed model training often fail to account for resource limitations in these devices. In this study, we introduce a new algorithm for model training that is both distributed and utilizes asynchronous techniques. This algorithm, called FedBuff, builds on a federated learning framework and employs a buffer to store models from individual devices, allowing for more efficient model updates. Our analysis shows that this algorithm can achieve the same level of model accuracy as traditional methods but with significantly reduced gradient computations. We also explore the benefits of this algorithm in the context of mobile and IoT applications, where it can reduce the number of devices that need to participate in model training while maintaining the same level of accuracy. Numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of this algorithm in terms of both model accuracy and computational efficiency.

This research paper introduces the concept of transfer learning in the context of automatic speech recognition (ASR), specifically focusing on applying a pre-trained ASR model from a high-level language to a low-resource language with a different writing system. The team developed a novel approach called Cross-Lingual Transfer (CLT) to facilitate this process. The CLT approach involves adapting the ASR model's parameters to a target language using a set of randomly generated data, followed by fine-tuning with a small set of real parallel sentences. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated through experiments on the Vietnamese-English Switchboard dataset, showing significant improvements in word error rate compared to traditional transfer methods. The team also applied the CLT approach to another language pair, Thai-English Switchboard, and achieved similar results. The research code is available on GitHub.

This paper introduces a novel approach to navigation for marine robots using
Gaussian Process TD Learning (GP-TDL). Unlike traditional methods, our approach
leverages the sparsity of the GP to reduce computational costs, enabling real-time
operation. We employ the inducing point-based sparse approximation of the GP to
achieve this efficiency. To address the challenge of limited state space
observations, we incorporate a new temporal difference learning algorithm that
effectively utilizes past observations. Our approach is tested in a simulation
using the Oceanic Robot, and the results demonstrate its ability to provide safe
navigation while reducing computational costs.

We have developed a unified framework for anisotropic two-fluid stellar configurations within General Relativity, where both fluids share the same anisotropic nature. This framework allows for the combination of previously established matching techniques for planar and spherical interfaces, enabling the construction of complex objects consisting of up to three distinct layers. As a concrete example, we have created a two-fluid model with an outer barotropic layer and a core exhibiting anisotropy, both conforming to specific anharmonic oscillators. This model can be matched with various exterior solutions, and we have analyzed the stability of these configurations using both adiabatic and dynamical criteria. Additionally, we have investigated the impact of anisotropy on the maximum mass and radius of these objects.

This paper investigates few-shot domain adaptation in Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) through the use of meta-learning, addressing the challenge of limited labeled data in new target domains. We propose a novel framework that leverages source domain knowledge and adapts to target domains with minimal labeled data. Our approach consists of two main components: a source domain model trained using a large-scale dataset, and a lightweight adapter module that can be fine-tuned on target domains. We evaluate our approach on the IWSLT 2017 and 2018 few-shot domain adaptation tasks and achieve state-of-the-art results. We also conduct an ablation study to analyze the effectiveness of our approach.

This paper investigates the allocation of indivisible goods among self-interested agents who can either accept or reject each item. We establish that in a setting where agents aim to maximize their accepted items, there exists a mechanism that guarantees social welfare lower bounds of 0.594 times the optimal for three agents and 0.667 times the optimal for four or more agents, while any other mechanism faces significant challenges in achieving these welfare guarantees. We also examine a scenario where agents can split their effort between accepting and rejecting items, demonstrating that similar welfare bounds can be achieved. In contrast, we prove that any mechanism must allow for allocations that result in social welfare as low as one-third of the optimal in the case of two or more self-interested agents.

UGC 8839 is a rare starburst galaxy with an exceptionally low rate of stellar rotation instability. A unique feature of this galaxy is a compact, gas-rich central disk that is 5-6 kiloparsecs in diameter and exhibits a very low rate of rotation instability. This small disk is surrounded by a larger, gas-poor outer region. A powerful jet from the galaxy's center is observed, and it is hypothesized that this jet is responsible for clearing out the outer region of the galaxy, thereby confining star formation to the protected central disk. This scenario is similar to what was previously proposed for another galaxy, NGC 1275. A potential link between the galaxy's central jet and its starburst activity is also noted.

A lattice QCD calculation has been conducted to determine two-quark correlation functions within a pion at multiple lattice spacings using the Wilson gauge action and staggered fermions. The correlation functions are found to be consistent with predictions made by chiral perturbation theory, particularly in the context of isospin breaking effects.

The relationship between a protoplanetary disk and its parent star is
fundamental to understanding planet formation. To better understand this
relationship, we must first characterize the properties of these systems,
including the behavior of the host star. In this study, we investigate the
variability of the X-ray luminosity of XX Cha over a period of 1.5 years,
using X-ray data from the Chandra observatory. We found that XX Cha exhibits
significant luminosity variability, with fluctuations of up to three orders of
magnitude, which is not typical for T Tauri stars. We also observed that the
variability in X-ray luminosity is not reflected in the optical spectrum,
which suggests that the accretion flow is decoupled from the corona. We
further found that the variability in X-ray luminosity is not uniform across
different energy bands, with soft X-rays showing more variability than hard
X-rays. This may be due to the presence of an extended structure, such as a
disk wind, that affects the X-ray spectrum. We also investigated the impact
of this variability on the relationship between X-ray luminosity and accretion
rate, which is not linear and may be influenced by the variability in X-ray
luminosity. This has important implications for studies of planet formation,
